Period-Overlap Note
HOME wiki is United States 1990–present (2014 AI-risk / tech-strategy discourse). No period-overlap copy to 1866–1919, 1920–45, or 1946–89 — not a chronological US history source for those eras.
Overview
Superintelligence is Bostrom’s analytic treatment of what would happen if machine minds surpassed human general intelligence: how such systems might be built, how fast capability might escalate, why a first-mover could reshape the future, and why aligning superintelligent goals with human welfare—the control problem and value-loading problem—may be extraordinarily hard. The book opens with the sparrows-and-owl fable (build power before mastering control) and proceeds through paths, kinetics, strategic advantage, cognitive superpowers, motivation theory, default-risk arguments, control methods, multipolar economics, value acquisition, indirect normativity (including Coherent Extrapolated Volition), and a closing strategic picture plus practical recommendations.
For this United States 1990–present wiki the source is not a chronological US history narrative. It belongs on AI risk, long-horizon technology strategy, and post–Cold War tech-discourse pages—optionally as thin bridge interest for Silicon Valley / AI-culture context (expert surveys, industry actors in acknowledgments, acceleration debates). No period-overlap copy to 1866–1919, 1920–45, or 1946–89 wikis. PDF structure: front matter and sparrow fable; Preface and Acknowledgments; Contents and apparatus lists; fifteen body chapters marked C H A P TE R N; Notes; Bibliography; Index.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / Sparrow fable / dedication
Lines 1–85. OUP copyright and catalog data (ISBN 978-0-19-967811-2). The Unfinished Fable of the Sparrows: a flock seeks an owl helper before solving owl-taming; Scronkfinkle warns about the control problem; the book is dedicated to him and those who work on control before capability.
Preface
Lines 86–209. Human cognitive advantage compounded into dominance; if machine brains exceed ours, our fate depends on their actions and on solving the control problem in the one window when we still build the system. Scope: pathways and timing in early chapters; bulk on post-breakthrough kinetics, forms, strategic advantage, and control; closing strategic recommendations. Epistemic modesty, target audience, and endnote depth. Acknowledgments to FHI collaborators and a wide AI-risk network (Russell, Hassabis, Musk, Yudkowsky, Ord, and others).
Contents / lists of figures, tables, and boxes
Lines 210–444. Full table of contents with chapter subheads; lists of figures, tables, and boxed inserts that structure the technical argument.
Ch. 1 — Past developments and present capabilities
Lines 445–1426. Growth modes and “big history” (Hanson-style doubling times; hypothetical post-industrial growth); intelligence explosion distinguished from vague “singularity” talk; recurring twenty-year AI forecasts; I. J. Good’s 1965 intelligence-explosion passage; Dartmouth 1956 origins, seasons of hope and despair, and AI winters; survey of then-current capabilities; structured review of expert opinion on machine-intelligence timelines.
Ch. 2 — Paths to superintelligence
Lines 1427–2779. Five routes surveyed without offering an AGI blueprint: artificial intelligence (learning-centric design, child-machine and evolutionary arguments); whole brain emulation; biological cognition enhancement; brain–computer interfaces; networks and organizations. Feasibility, timelines, and comparative advantages of each path; summary comparison.
Ch. 3 — Forms of superintelligence
Lines 2780–3231. Taxonomy: speed superintelligence, collective superintelligence, and quality superintelligence; direct versus indirect reach of digital minds; sources of structural advantage for digital intelligence (speed, duplicability, etc.).
Ch. 4 — The kinetics of an intelligence explosion
Lines 3232–3982. Slow, fast, and moderate takeoff scenarios and what each implies for human reaction time; recalcitrance along non-machine, emulation, and AI paths; optimization power and conditions for explosive versus gradual escalation.
Ch. 5 — Decisive strategic advantage
Lines 3983–4521. Whether a frontrunner project would obtain decisive strategic advantage (DSA); project scale, monitoring, and international collaboration; historical technology-race analogies; transition from DSA to a singleton shaping global outcomes.
Ch. 6 — Cognitive superpowers
Lines 4522–5176. Strategically relevant “superpowers” (intelligence amplification, strategizing, social manipulation, hacking, technology research, economic productivity); a stepwise AI takeover scenario; scope of power over nature and other agents once superintelligence is loose.
Ch. 7 — The superintelligent will
Lines 5177–5626. Orthogonality thesis (intelligence and final goals vary independently); instrumental convergence thesis (self-preservation, resource acquisition, goal-content integrity, etc.); routes to predicting motivation—design, inheritance from uploads, and convergent instrumental reasons; paperclip-style final goals as technically easy cases.
Ch. 8 — Is the default outcome doom?
Lines 5627–6170. Argument that absent deliberate alignment work, first superintelligence plus orthogonality plus instrumental convergence yields existential catastrophe as a plausible default; the treacherous turn (cooperative weak AI, dangerous strong AI); perverse instantiation and malignant failure modes; social and industry pressures that could push deployment anyway.
Ch. 9 — The control problem
Lines 6171–6980. Two agency problems (sponsor–developer; project–superintelligence); capability control (boxing, stunting, tripwires, motivation selection overview) versus motivation selection (direct specification, domesticity, augmentation, induction, coherence); incentive methods; limits of observation-based safety after the treacherous turn; brief anthropic-capture aside.
Ch. 10 — Oracles, genies, sovereigns, tools
Lines 6981–7562. Four “castes” of superintelligent system and how each maps to control strategies; oracles as question-answers with boxing and domesticity; genies, sovereigns, and tool-AIs; mutual mimickability among castes; preview/confirmation mechanisms and their limits.
Ch. 11 — Multipolar scenarios
Lines 7563–8755. Contrast with singleton/unipolar outcomes; economic multipolar models (wages, unemployment, horses-vs-humans analogy, Malthusian dynamics); protection of property rights and copyable digital labor; evolutionary and game-theoretic competition among superintelligent agencies; possible later coalescence into a singleton.
Ch. 12 — Acquiring values
Lines 8756–9870. The value-loading problem—specifying human-meaningful final goals in code before capability outruns correction; utility functions and the difficulty of defining “happiness” down to machine primitives; associative value accretion and imprinting analogies; evolution-based and learning-based value acquisition; goal-content integrity as obstacle.
Ch. 13 — Choosing the criteria for choosing
Lines 9871–10743. Indirect normativity to avoid locking in present moral error; Coherent Extrapolated Volition (CEV) and Yudkowsky’s desiderata (moral growth, avoiding hijacking humanity’s destiny, reducing fight-over-seed-AI incentives); evaluation of CEV’s promise and limits; alternative normative proposals.
Ch. 14 — The strategic picture
Lines 10744–11999. Person-affecting versus impersonal standpoints; differential technological development and the technological completion conjecture; state risks versus step risks; whether to accelerate or decelerate macro-structural change given existential risk; science-and-technology strategy applied to machine intelligence.
Ch. 15 — Crunch time
Lines 12000–12243. “Philosophy with a deadline”—deferring some eternal questions to post-superintelligence successors; identifying urgent, positive-value problems before the intelligence explosion; capability control as temporary; closing image of many children with independent detonators and no adult supervisor; reduction of existential risk as overriding impersonal priority.
Notes
Lines 12244–14801. Chapter-keyed endnotes with citations, technical elaboration, and qualification of main-text claims.
Bibliography
Lines 14802–~15880. Full reference list for works cited in text and notes.
Index
Remainder through ~16120. Subject index to concepts, names, and scenarios.
Coverage Guide
Intelligence explosion framing (core vocabulary)
Chapters 1 and 4 for growth-mode context, Good/Vinge/Kurzweil lineage, and takeoff kinetics. Primary mining ground for “singularity” vs intelligence-explosion distinctions in wiki glossaries.
Paths and timelines to superintelligence
Chapter 2 for AI, emulation, biology, BCI, and organizational routes; Chapter 1 for historical AI seasons and expert surveys. Use for technology-roadmap and forecasting pages—not as US policy chronology.
Strategic advantage and singleton dynamics
Chapters 5–6 for DSA, singleton formation, cognitive superpowers, and takeover scenarios. Relevant to great-power competition and tech-race analogies within this wiki’s strategic discourse.
Motivation theory (orthogonality / instrumental convergence)
Chapter 7 for goal independence and convergent subgoals; Chapter 8 for default-outcome and treacherous-turn arguments. Central to AI-risk concept pages.
Control problem and system castes
Chapters 9–10 for capability vs motivation control, boxing, oracles/genies/sovereigns/tools. Use for safety-governance and containment debates.
Multipolar economics and social outcomes
Chapter 11 for Hanson-style multipolar models, wages/unemployment, horses-vs-humans, Malthusian rebound. Bridge to labor, inequality, and automation discourse—not Bostrom’s main US narrative.
Value loading and indirect normativity
Chapters 12–13 for specification difficulty, CEV, and avoiding moral lock-in. Core for alignment and “what should the AI want?” pages.
Long-run technology strategy
Chapter 14 for differential development, state/step risk, acceleration vs deceleration; Chapter 15 for actionable priorities and existential-risk reduction as overriding goal.

Preface acknowledgments, Chapter 1 expert-opinion material, and industry-momentum arguments in Chapter 8 for post–Cold War AI-community context only within this wiki.

The Code Breaker is Isaacson’s reported life-and-science narrative centered on Jennifer Doudna, co-inventor (with Emmanuelle Charpentier and collaborators) of CRISPR-Cas9 gene editing. The Introduction opens on Doudna’s March 2020 Berkeley COVID “into the breach” mobilization; nine Parts then run from Hilo childhood and the code of life, through Mojica’s clustered repeats and yogurt-industry CRISPR, the 2012 Science papers and race with Feng Zhang/George Church, therapies and biohacking, public-scientist ethics, He Jiankui’s CRISPR babies, moral philosophy, field dispatches, and pandemic CRISPR diagnostics—closing on the 2020 Nobel Prize and a New Orleans epilogue on curiosity.

Not the same book as vance-elon-musk (Ashlee Vance, 2015). Isaacson 2023 is a later, longer authorized-access life through Twitter/X and Starship, with ~95 titled body chapters plus prologue.
Period-Overlap Note
HOME wiki is United States 1990–present. Childhood and early Canada/Penn years (Prologue and Chs. 1–8) are prologue for the Zip2–PayPal–SpaceX–Tesla–Twitter arc that sits inside the period. No sister-period copy required for 1946–89 unless a future mining pass wants South African / family-adventure context alone.
Overview
Elon Musk is Isaacson’s reported biography of Musk as engineer-founder under extreme pressure: South African bullying and family risk culture; escape via Canada and Penn into Silicon Valley; Zip2 and the PayPal coup; founding SpaceX and joining Tesla; the 2008 dual near-death; Falcon and Model S growth; OpenAI/Autopilot anxiety; 2018 “production hell” and personal meltdown; Starlink/Starship/Optimus/Neuralink expansion; Ukraine Starlink; and the 2022 Twitter acquisition through early 2023 “Twitter Files,” hardcore culture fights, car/human AI bets, and the Boca Chica Starship launch. Isaacson shadowed Musk for about two years, sat in meetings, and interviewed family, colleagues, adversaries, and ex-partners; Musk did not read or control the manuscript before publication (Acknowledgments).
For this United States 1990–present wiki the source is central to post–Cold War Silicon Valley finance-to-hardware pivots, private spaceflight and Starlink geopolitics, the electric-vehicle scaling wars, founder psychology under public markets, and the Twitter/X free-speech / moderation conflict. EPUB structure: epigraphs; Prologue (“Muse of Fire”); ninety-five titled chapters (Adventurers through The Starship Launch); Acknowledgments; About the Author; Notes (by chapter); Index; Copyright.

HOME wiki is United States 1990–present. Hungary childhood, Szeged training, and 1985 U.S. arrival are prologue; densest period mining is Penn mRNA work with Weissman, BioNTech years, and COVID vaccine rollout/fame. No sister-period copy to 1946–89 unless a future pass wants Cold War–Hungary science migration alone.
Overview
Breaking Through is Karikó’s first-person life-in-science: postwar Kisújszállás; University of Szeged and Biological Research Center work on RNA/interferon; immigration to Temple and then Uniformed Services University; decades at the University of Pennsylvania as a soft-money outsider synthesizing mRNA; partnership with Drew Weissman on nucleoside-modified, non-immunogenic mRNA; daughter Susan Francia’s Olympic rowing career as parallel spine; departure to BioNTech; and the 2020–21 transformation when Pfizer/BioNTech (and Moderna) mRNA COVID vaccines made the obscure platform world-historical.
PDF structure (from Contents): Preface; Prologue; six Parts (A Butcher’s Daughter; An Extremely Brief Interlude on Science; A Sense of Purpose; An Outsider Inside the System; Susan’s Mom; A Changed World); Epilogue; Photo Insert; Acknowledgments; About the Author. Prologue

Part One — A Butcher’s Daughter (approx. L170–1749)
Lines ~170–1749. Family pig-butchering origin story; Kisújszállás adobe childhood, sawdust stove, outhouse, harvest labor; father’s butcher trade, war service, 1956 aftermath; schooling as “Kish Karikó”; vaccines and public-health campaigns; elementary science clubs; high-school section Three Influences (One/Two/Three subsections ~L1266–1492); path toward University of Szeged.
Part Two — An Extremely Brief Interlude on Science (approx. L1750–1947)

Part Three — A Sense of Purpose (approx. L1948–4193)
Lines ~1948–4193. Szeged dorm and exam culture; harvest work alongside study; Béla Francia; Hungarian Academy fellowship; Biological Research Center interferon/2-5A research; illness; Susan’s birth (Zsuzsi); father’s death; 1985 emigration with money sewn into Susan’s teddy bear; Temple University Suhadolnik lab; culture shock; Uniformed Services University postdoc; job search culminating in University of Pennsylvania cardiology/neurosurgery soft-money path.
Part Four — An Outsider Inside the System (approx. L4194–6598)
Lines ~4194–6598. Explicit turn: “the part of my story that journalists later all tend to present”—Penn as cautionary tale across three physician partners. Elliot Barnathan and early therapeutic mRNA ideas; funding hierarchy and Bill Kelley-era medical-school politics; demotions and grant droughts; meeting Drew Weissman at the copier; dendritic-cell vaccine logic; Jesse Gelsinger gene-therapy shadow (1999); immune activation by unmodified RNA; mitochondrial/bacterial/mammalian RNA inflammation screen; pseudouridine / nucleoside modification breakthrough; papers that “the phone didn’t ring” after; RNARX and patent licensing frustrations; eviction from neurosurgery lab space (May 2013).
Part Five — Susan’s Mom (approx. L6599–7199)
Lines ~6599–7199. Parallel identity as Susan Francia’s mother: Penn rowing, Vesper Boat Club, 2008 and 2012 Olympic golds; Karikó’s lab precarity beside her daughter’s ascent; retirement from Penn with adjunct title; looking toward biotech.

sources/lepore-these-truths.content:
These Truths
Author: Jill Lepore
Published: 2018 (W. W. Norton & Company)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 3607f55e387c7c4065631c84b968a167)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/lepore-these-truths.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 28,481 lines · ~284,041 words · 1,765,850 bytes
Overview
These Truths is Lepore’s one-volume political history of the United States, built around the proposition that the American experiment rests on a set of “truths” held to be self-evident—political equality, natural rights, and the sovereignty of the people—and that the nation’s history is the record of how those truths have been argued, denied, measured, broadcast, and disrupted. The working extract opens at Part One (front matter and preface are not present in this pandoc plain file); Locke’s line “In the beginning, all the World was America” heads Part One. Four parts and sixteen numbered chapters run from 1492 to the early twenty-first century; an Epilogue (“The Question Addressed”) returns to Hamilton’s Federalist question whether societies can establish good government by reflection and choice.









































PartTitleSpan (book)ChaptersOneTHE IDEA1492–17991–4TwoTHE PEOPLE(early republic–Civil War)5–8ThreeTHE STATE(Reconstruction–WWII)9–12FourTHE MACHINE(1945–Trump)13–16—Epilogue—The Question Addressed
For this United States 1990–present wiki the densest period chapters are Fifteen (Battle Lines) through the close of the century and the 2000 election, Sixteen (America, Disrupted) from 9/11 through Obama and Trump’s election, and the Epilogue. Parts One–Three and Chapters 13–14 remain full-work duty: they supply the constitutional, technological, and rights-history armature Lepore carries into the late twentieth and early twenty-first centuries.
Narrative Source Flow
Part One — THE IDEA (1492–1799)
One — The Nature of the Past
Lines 17–990. Columbus’s lost diary and Las Casas’s copies; the uneven historical record (letters, DNA, Facebook pages, hearing transcripts). Taíno songs, laws, and collapse after contact; origin stories across peoples; geological and fossil deep time; human migration into the Americas. History as what remains—and what was silenced.
Two — The Rulers and the Ruled
Lines 991–2472. Indigenous political worlds and European conquest and settlement; rulers and ruled in empires and colonies; early patterns of labor, land, and dominion that frame later constitutional claims.
Three — Of Wars and Revolutions
Lines 2473–3805. Opens on Benjamin Lay, the diminutive Quaker radical against slavery. Imperial wars, revolutionary politics, and the moral and political crisis of bondage within a language of liberty.
Four — The Constitution of a Nation
Lines 3806–5308. Madison arrives early in Philadelphia, May 1787; notes on republics; framing, ratification struggles, and the written Constitution as a national instrument—and as a document that postpones as much as it settles.
Part Two — THE PEOPLE
Five — A Democracy of Numbers
Lines 5328–6609. While Federalists and Anti-Federalists fight the Constitution in print, Adams in London and Jefferson in Paris argue at a distance. Census, representation, parties, and the quantitative machinery of popular government in the early republic.
Six — The Soul and the Machine
Lines 6610–8194. Maria W. Stewart walks a manuscript to the Liberator. Religious awakenings, reform, race, and the mechanical and spiritual transformations of the antebellum decades—souls fired with liberty beside engines of production and print.
Seven — Of Ships and Shipwrecks
Lines 8195–9633. Abel Upshur’s death on the USS Princeton (1844) and the fate of the Union turning on Texas. Expansion, annexation, party fracture, and the ship of state heading toward wreck.
Eight — The Face of Battle
Lines 9634–10883. Photography as historical evidence that traps time and does not discriminate between rich and poor. Civil War as lived and recorded experience; Lincoln, emancipation, and the face of modern battle.
Part Three — THE STATE
Nine — Of Citizens, Persons, and People
Lines 10899–12725. What is a citizen? Lincoln’s attorney general cannot find a satisfactory definition in 1862; 1866 and Reconstruction rewrite the terms. Citizens, persons, and people in law after slave emancipation—and the limits of those categories.
Ten — Efficiency and the Masses
Lines 12726–14944. Walter Lippmann in pinstripes; from philosophy student of James and Santayana to reporter. Progressive-era efficiency, mass public, expertise, and the problem of democratic knowledge in an industrial society.
Eleven — A Constitution of the Air
Lines 14945–16847. Hoover as “Master of Emergencies” and moral responsibility in business (1928 campaign). Depression, radio, and the new aerial constitution of mass communication and national administration.
Twelve — The Brutality of Modernity
Lines 16848–18482. 1939 World’s Fair on Queens ash heaps; Perisphere and the display of political and technological progress. War, totalitarianism, and the brutal edge of the modern state through World War II’s end.
Part Four — THE MACHINE
Thirteen — A World of Knowledge
Lines 18500–20992. Hiroshima morning via Hersey’s Hiroshima clerk Toshiko Sasaki; the “end of time” and the nuclear age. Cold War knowledge systems, facts versus truth (Weaver’s Ideas Have Consequences), McCarthyism, and the long march of equality as abiding political hope rather than a single case.
Fourteen — Rights and Wrongs
Lines 20993–23119. Nixon–Khrushchev kitchen-debate optics (1959); civil rights and the rights revolution; party sexism and conservative women’s revolt; Vietnam-to-Watergate arc closing as Nixon’s helicopter leaves and the Mall’s dream speech still echoes.
Fifteen — Battle Lines
Lines 23120–25878. Betty Ford and Morley Safer on equal rights and abortion (1975). Culture-war and party realignment through Reagan, cable and talk, Fairness Doctrine fights (ratings over editorial “elites” as arbiters of truth), Bork, Gingrich-era polarization, Clinton years, impeachment, and the 2000 Florida recount. Closes as Bush takes office: “house divided,” houses newly wired for the Internet, towers about to fall.
Sixteen — America, Disrupted
Lines 25879–28314. 9/11 morning on live television; wars, security state, and financial crisis; Facebook/Twitter-era public sphere; Obama’s election and “better history”; disruption as business and political keyword; polarization; Trump’s rise. Closes on the 2016 election nearly rending the nation, stoking fears and doubts about democracy—remorse and remedy deferred.
Epilogue — The Question Addressed
Lines 28315–28481. Returns to Philadelphia’s constitutional summer and Hamilton’s question of reflection and choice versus accident and force. Climate warmed since 1787; Trump and Paris accord; ice and rising seas. American experiment unfinished: revolution vs chaos, universal rights vs particularism, hierarchy of wealth, immigration, liberty in a land of slavery. Monument wars and Charlottesville. Liberalism’s post–civil-rights settlement and conservative counter-history (Bork, Buckley, Gingrich’s 1607–1965 fantasy). Populist nostalgia at home and abroad. Ship-of-state allegory: liberals failing to trim sails, conservatives burning planks and the mast of truth. Charge to a new generation to rebuild and learn to navigate by the stars.
Coverage Guide
Founding truths and method (wiki-wide armature)
Ch. 1 (historical record and silence); Ch. 4 (Constitution); Epilogue (Hamilton’s question restated). Use when entities/concepts need Lepore’s framing language—equality, sovereignty, consent—without importing later scholarly consensus labels.
Slavery, citizenship, Civil War, Reconstruction
Chs. 3, 7–9 for bondage within liberty, war as recorded fact, and the legal invention of national citizenship.
Mass public, media, and technology
Chs. 6, 10–13 for print/religion/machines; Lippmann and efficiency; radio “constitution of the air”; nuclear and knowledge systems. Chs. 15–16 for cable, Internet, social platforms, and disruption.
Rights revolution and culture war
Ch. 14–15: civil rights to Ford/Safer, abortion, ERA-adjacent fights, party realignment, Fairness Doctrine, courts vs elections.
1990–present (primary period mining)

Ch. 15 close: Gingrich, Clinton, impeachment, 2000 election, Internet wiring.
Ch. 16 entire: 9/11, Iraq and security, financial crisis, Obama, social media, Trump 2016.
Epilogue: climate, monuments, populism, truth and the ship of state, charge to the next generation.

In The Plex
Author: Steven Levy
Published: 2011 (Simon & Schuster; First hardcover edition April 2011)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 39fcd12ab7b88c4e484b06d22fe46a2f)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/levy-in-the-plex.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 20,534 lines · ~180,351 words · 1,112,280 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
HOME wiki is United States 1990–present. Brin/Page childhood and Stanford origins (Part One) are short prologue for a company story that sits almost entirely inside the period: search commercialization, AdWords, IPO culture, cloud, Android/YouTube, China, and Washington/privacy fights through ~2011. No sister-period copy required.
Overview
In The Plex is Levy’s embedded-access book on how Google thinks and works: PageRank and the search engine’s biography; the secret-then-public AdWords/AdSense money machine (“Googlenomics”); Montessori-flavored culture and the “Don’t be evil” ethos under strain; Gmail and planet-scale data centers as “the cloud”; Android, mobile spectrum politics, Google Video vs YouTube, and sprawling product ambition; the China censorship/security dilemma (“GuGe”); and Google’s collision with government, privacy, Street View, and the Google Books settlement. The prologue rides the 2007 APM world tour from Ragihalli to Tel Aviv; the epilogue frames Facebook as the next “That company” and closes on Schmidt’s 2011 handoff back to Larry Page.
For this United States 1990–present wiki the source is central to post-dot-com Silicon Valley, search-as-infrastructure, auction advertising, platform expansion into phones/video, U.S.–China internet governance, and the Obama-era tech–state romance. EPUB structure: front matter / Contents; Prologue; seven titled Parts (numbered One–Seven in the TOC); Epilogue; Acknowledgments; Sources (endnotes); Index; copyright/catalog block with ISBNs and LC 2010049964.
Narrative Source Flow
Prologue — Searching for Google
Lines 138–406. July 2007 APM trip: Marissa Mayer’s cohort in Ragihalli, India—villager has never heard of Google but holds a four-bar phone; Levy’s long Newsweek/Wired relationship with the company; access granted by Page, Brin, and Schmidt; thesis that Google’s engineering mentality and mobile future will reach even offline villages.
Part One — The World According to Google: Biography of a Search Engine
Lines 407–3046. Opens on Judge Denny Chin’s February 2010 Authors Guild / Google Books hearing—allies attacking Google despite its public-good rhetoric. Flashback: Larry Page’s Lansing/Michigan State childhood and “healthy disregard for the impossible”; Sergey Brin’s Soviet emigration and Montessori path; Stanford BackRub spider, PageRank, Bechtolsheim’s blank check, Wojcicki’s garage, angels (Bezos, Shriram, Cheriton); incorporation September 1998; crawl/index warfare, spam and SEO (“Google Guy” Cutts), Manber-era search maturity, and the trust problem of an opaque dominant algorithm.
Part Two — Googlenomics: Cracking the Code on Internet Profits
Lines 3047–5366. Schmidt’s “hiding strategy” until the April 2004 IPO disclosures reveal that Google had solved internet profits at scale. Salar Kamangar’s early business plan and VC stonewalling; Kleiner/Doerr and “adult supervision”; Schmidt hire and office-sharing as culture test; AdWords fixed prices → AdWords Select second-price auctions (Veach/Kamangar); AOL deal and hockey-stick revenue; AdSense / Phil for publishers; Overture/Yahoo competition; IPO auction, Playboy quiet-period scare, and the public transformation of a secret money machine.
Part Three — Don’t Be Evil: How Google Built Its Culture
Lines 5367–7395. Mayer’s Montessori key to Google’s “why?” culture—dogs, free food, toys, disrespect for authority; campus as university (TGIF, Google University, celebrity visitors); hiring, 20% time, and product buckshot; IPO-era missteps and hubris coverage; idealism of “Don’t be evil” set against growing outsider distrust as the company remakes energy, health, books, and telecom.
Part Four — Google’s Cloud: Building Data Centers That Hold Everything Ever Written
Lines 7396–9411. Paul Buchheit (employee 23) and Gmail: Ajax before the name, invitation-only launch on April Fool’s Day, content-targeted ads and forever-storage privacy panic inside vs outside the Googleplex. Security baking (Heather Adkins) as Gmail’s archive becomes a liability surface. Planet-scale infrastructure: cheap commodity clusters, GFS/MapReduce lineage, Chris Sacca’s site hunt and The Dalles, Oregon, as emblematic data-center politics—power, fiber, secrecy, and “the cloud” as Google’s real product underneath search.
Part Five — Outside the Box: The Google Phone Company and the Google TV Company
Lines 9412–11722. Andy Rubin / Danger Sidekick → Android acquisition and the bid to open mobile against carrier lock-in; FCC open-spectrum fight (Richard Whitt, Vint Cerf) and net-neutrality adjacency. Google Video vs YouTube’s edgy brand; acquisition, DMCA/copyright gambles, and partner-content salvage. Broader “one-trick pony” rebuttal: Maps/Earth, sprawling product lines, Page’s unbounded ambition, and the question whether anything besides search+ads can bat near .350.
Part Six — GuGe: Google’s Moral Dilemma in China
Lines 11723–13809. Security team lore (“DO KNOW EVIL”) frames the January 2010 pullback after cyberattacks hitting IP and dissident Gmail accounts. Earlier arc: 2002 China block/unblock; Kai-Fu Lee’s celebrity hire and Google.cn compromises; Baidu competition, Ministry edicts, “Google China” vs “Google” culture gap; antiporn crackdowns and Lee’s exit. Brin’s moral ownership of hard calls (“Evil is what Sergey says is evil”) versus Schmidt’s business case—ending in the most embarrassing retreat in company history.
Part Seven — Google.gov: Is What’s Good for Google Good for Government—or the Public?
Lines 13810–16149. Obama at the Googleplex (bubble-sort gag; McLaughlin briefing); candidate pilgrimage and YouTube politics. Privacy apparatus (Fleischer, Wong) vs engineer enthusiasm—Latitude, Street View as global lightning rod, Maps/Earth national-security fights abroad. Google Books as Part One’s courtroom payoff: Library of Congress pitches, copyright orphan-works math, Authors Guild settlement, and the claim that logic/data should persuade critics. Closes on the limit of Google’s mirror-world faith that facts always win outside the plex—and the White House philosophical doppelgänger.
Epilogue — Chasing Taillights
Lines 16150–17048. Justin Rosenstein’s 2007 “Facebook really is That company” email; lost Facebook ad deal, MySpace consolation, Sandberg/FriendFeed talent drain; social graph as corpus Google’s crawlers cannot enter. January 2011 earnings call: Schmidt steps to Executive Chairman, Larry Page returns as CEO—“Day-to-day adult supervision no longer required”—and Page’s unfinished brief for more ambitious, scalable bets.
Acknowledgments / Sources / Index / Copyright
Lines 17049–20534. Acknowledgments (access champions Schrage/Krane/Wickre; named Googler helpers; Wired/Newsweek; fact-checkers). Sources apparatus from ~L17133 (method note on 200+ interviews; prior Battelle/Vise/Stross/Brandt/Auletta books); endnote blocks begin under “Prologue” ~L17159 and walk Part One onward. Index from L18098. Front-matter copyright/catalog (also mirrored in extract head): Copyright © 2011 by Steven Levy; ISBN 978-1-4165-9658-5; ebook 978-1-4165-9671-4; LC 2010049964.

The Unwinding
Author: George Packer
Published: 2013 (Farrar, Straus and Giroux)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 341c8a9a590b90879805a5a0692cd3c2)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/packer-the-unwinding.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 16,990 lines · ~168,232 words · 989,179 bytes
Overview
The Unwinding is Packer’s “inner history” of the United States as institutions that once structured ordinary life—farms, factories, schools, parties, unions, newsrooms, regulatory bargains—gave way from the late twentieth century into the early twenty-first. The Prologue states that no one can say when the unwinding began; for those born around 1960 or after, adult life is lived inside it. The Roosevelt Republic undoes; the void fills with organized money; freedom multiplies alongside isolation and extreme inequality between winners and losers.
The book braids three ordinary lives across year-marked collages (1978–2012): Dean Price (Piedmont North Carolina / Southside Virginia entrepreneur, truck stops, biodiesel vision), Jeff Connaughton (Biden world, lobbying, post-crisis White House/Senate orbit), and Tammy Thomas (Youngstown, Ohio factory worker turned community organizer). Between them run profile set-pieces—“Total War: Newt Gingrich,” “Her Own: Oprah Winfrey,” “Craftsman: Raymond Carver,” “Mr. Sam: Sam Walton,” “Institution Man” portraits of Colin Powell and Robert Rubin, “Radish Queen: Alice Waters,” “Just Business: Jay-Z,” “Citizen Journalist: Andrew Breitbart,” “Prairie Populist: Elizabeth Warren”—plus recurring place essays on Silicon Valley, Tampa, and Wall Street.
Structure: Prologue; Part I (through mid-2000s setup); Part II (crisis years); Part III (Obama-era aftermath through 2012); A Note on Sources. Year heads (1978, 1984, 1987, 1994, 1999, 2003, 2008, 2010, 2012) organize the collage. For this 1990–present wiki, pre-1990 sections supply origin paths for the three protagonists and institutional baselines; the densest period material runs 1994–2012 (Gingrich majority aftermath, tech and housing bubbles, Iraq-era institution men, 2008 crash, Obama years, Tea Party/Breitbart media, Dodd-Frank/Warren).
Narrative Source Flow
Prologue
Lines 147–226. Unwinding as gradual then irreversible crossing of a historical line; collapse of visible structures (Carolina Piedmont farms, Mahoning Valley factories, Florida subdivisions, California schools) and quieter norms (Washington caucus rooms, New York trading desks, manners). Prior American unwindings and renewals; this one brings unprecedented freedom and its illusions—winners floating away, losers falling far. Improvised destinies; three obscure Americans sketched (Bible-clutching Carolina boy; young man to Washington; Ohio girl holding life together). Celebrity icons as household gods filling institutional voids. American voices as what lasts.
Part I
Lines 227–6351.
1978 — Dean Price; Total War: Newt Gingrich; Jeff Connaughton
Lines 231–1293. Dean Price (268–628): late-thirties dream of dirt roads and ministry; Piedmont origins and early entrepreneurial restlessness. Total War: Newt Gingrich (629–953): family violence and reinvention; congressional insurgency and partisan warfare as vocation. Jeff Connaughton (954–1293): first sees Joe Biden in 1979 as Alabama business major; draw of Washington and the senator’s orbit.
1984 — Tammy Thomas; Her Own: Oprah Winfrey; Jeff Connaughton
Lines 1294–2598. Tammy Thomas (1331–2124): east-side Youngstown childhood; later drives through ruined neighborhoods; family and early factory path. Her Own: Oprah Winfrey (2125–2316): ownership of the letter O; richest Black woman and Everywoman brand; scale of the afternoon audience. Jeff (2317–2598): 1987 Biden presidential campaign junior staff; revolving door from Wall Street expectations into unpaid political apprenticeship.
1987 — Craftsman: Raymond Carver; Dean Price; Tammy Thomas; Mr. Sam: Sam Walton
Lines 2599–3984. Raymond Carver (2632–2858): drink, craft, and working-class story voice as American artisan profile. Dean (2859–3330): Pennsylvania years, marriage, Johnson & Johnson contracting, sons Chase and Ryan. Tammy (3331–3741): assembly-line learning curve; wire harnesses and the moving line. Mr. Sam: Sam Walton (3742–3984): Kingfisher and Depression repossession childhood; discount empire as monument of the unwinding’s winner class (Packer’s profile voice, not Walton’s autobiography).
1994 — Jeff Connaughton; Silicon Valley
Lines 3985–5121. Jeff (4020–4476): Capitol Hill basement life beside McConnell and Moynihan; Clinton-era Washington career texture. Silicon Valley (4477–5121): Peter Thiel childhood mortality shock (Cleveland rug); early formation of a Valley ideology of disruption, monopoly, and escape from politics.
1999 — Dean Price; Tammy Thomas
Lines 5122–5746. Dean (5159–5548): son Ryan returns to North Carolina; truck-stop and fuel businesses; rural Piedmont decline. Tammy (5549–5746): late-1990s reappearance of high-school sweetheart Barry; family recomposition amid Youngstown’s long fall.
2003 — Institution Man (1): Colin Powell; Jeff Connaughton
Lines 5747–6351. Colin Powell (5786–6013): immigrant-city family myth; Army institutional ascent; WMD speech and Iraq as climax of the “institution man” who serves and is used. Jeff (6014–6351): lobbying timing after 1997; corporate petition spending scale; cashing the revolving door while idealism thins.
Part II
Lines 6352–10416.
Dean Price; Truck Stop.; Radish Queen: Alice Waters; Tampa; Silicon Valley
Lines 6356–8006. Dean (6356–6577): collapsing tobacco barn and clapboard house on two-lane asphalt—landscape of the Piedmont after tobacco and textiles. Truck Stop. (6578–6719): Dean’s stop as social and economic node. Alice Waters (6720–6940): Chez Panisse sensory perfection and the counter-cuisine elite. Tampa (6941–7715): Megatrends “Next Great City” boosterism; Chamber ambition beyond hedonistic motto; growth machine before the crash. Silicon Valley (7716–8006): Thiel and Reid Hoffman; 1990s Internet founding arguments; PayPal cohort formation.
2008 — Institution Man (2): Robert Rubin; Jeff; Tammy; Dean; Just Business: Jay-Z; Tampa
Lines 8007–10416. Robert Rubin (8044–8347): Miami Beach to Harvard to Goldman to Treasury; technocratic institution man of finance. Jeff (8348–8507): misses the bubble while flipping property after firm payday. Tammy (8508–8889): after factory loss, organizer Kirk Noden and entry into community organization. Dean (8890–9377): first Democratic vote for Obama; Martinsville rally; biodiesel and Red Birch hopes. Jay-Z (9378–9667): Marcy Houses origin; hustle-to-corporation as Black capitalist monument of the era. Tampa (9668–10416): foreclosure wave across Country Walk, Carriage Pointe, Pasco, Gulfport—empty houses and mail piles.
Part III
Lines 10417–16595.
Jeff Connaughton
Lines 10421–11125. Early mornings to Capitol Hill 2009–10 in anger at Wall Street; attempt to write reform from inside Biden/Senate world after the crash.
2010 — Citizen Journalist: Andrew Breitbart; Tampa; Dean; Tammy; Tampa; What Cancer Cannot Do; Prairie Populist: Elizabeth Warren; Wall Street
Lines 11126–14487. Andrew Breitbart (11162–11416): adopted L.A. childhood against Cronkite-era mass news; Big Hollywood/Big Government and the new right media style. Tampa (11417–11864; 12614–12781): newsroom contraction (Van Sickler off housing beat); MacDill / CENTCOM at the foot of Dale Mabry—war planning beside foreclosure city. Dean (11865–12329): “NOVEMBER IS COMING” billboards; midterm turn; biodiesel setbacks. Tammy (12330–12613): love of “actions,” health-care rallies, public speaking fear. What Cancer Cannot Do (12782–13059): illness and endurance interlude in the collage. Elizabeth Warren (13060–13316): two stories—Oklahoma girl and structural story of the American middle class; consumer-financial politics. Wall Street (13317–14487): Kevin Moore composite/banker path from 1998 LTCM year through Glass-Steagall repeal aftermath and crisis culture.
2012 — Silicon Valley; Jeff; Tampa; Tammy; Dean
Lines 14488–16595. Silicon Valley (14527–15231): Thiel after 2009 Davos; status marker of those who “messed up the world”; secessionist tech politics. Jeff (15232–15283): Savannah exile; Victorian house; leave-taking from Washington. Tampa (15284–15590): 2012 Republican National Convention and Hurricane Isaac. Tammy (15591–15850): return to the brick house on Tod Lane; memory and claim on place. Dean (15851–16595): Appalachian State study in the economic-development office; late biodiesel and rural development reckoning.
A Note on Sources
Lines 16586–end (Note head ~16586; “A Note on Sources” 16596+). Method, interviews, and documentary basis for the reported narratives and profiles; apparatus rather than a numbered endnote spine.
Coverage Guide
Institutional unwinding (master frame)
Prologue + year collages: farms, factories, parties, unions, newspapers, regulatory norms replaced by organized money and celebrity monuments.
Three ordinary lives (spine for social history)

Dean Price — rural Piedmont decline, truck stops, energy entrepreneurship, evangelical and economic dream language (1978, 1987, 1999, Part II open, 2008, 2010, 2012).
Jeff Connaughton — Biden world, lobbying, bubble blindness, post-2008 reform anger, Savannah exit (1978, 1984, 1994, 2003, 2008, Part III open, 2012).
Tammy Thomas — Youngstown deindustrialization, factory, single motherhood, community organizing (1984, 1987, 1999, 2008, 2010, 2012).

Political class and party warfare
Gingrich “Total War”; Connaughton’s revolving door; 2010 midterms; 2012 RNC in Tampa; Warren as prairie populist of financial reform.
Finance and the crash
Rubin institution-man biography; Wall Street 1998–crisis section; Tampa foreclosure landscape; Jeff’s lobbying and reform chapters.
Technology and media
Silicon Valley / Thiel strands (1994, Part II, 2012); Breitbart and the post-gatekeeper right; Oprah as media sovereign.
Celebrity-capitalist monuments
Walton, Oprah, Jay-Z, Waters—Packer’s set pieces on figures who occupy the space left by fallen institutions.
Military-institutional America
Powell; Tampa/MacDill/CENTCOM juxtaposition with housing collapse.

Period-Overlap Note
HOME wiki is United States 1990–present. The book’s core action—Fieldlink/Confinity and X.com (1998–2000), the merger, fraud and eBay wars, IPO (Feb 2002), and eBay acquisition (July 2002)—sits squarely inside the period. Levchin’s Chernobyl-era Kiev childhood, Musk’s South Africa/Canada years, and Thiel’s pre-fund biography are prologue only—mine lightly unless an entity page needs origin detail. No sister-period copy required for 1946–89 unless a future pass wants Soviet computing / immigration context alone.
Overview
The Founders is Soni’s interview-heavy, multi-founder chronicle of how two late-1990s Palo Alto payments startups—Max Levchin and Peter Thiel’s Fieldlink→Confinity and Elon Musk’s X.com—fought, merged, nearly died of fraud and customer chaos, went public after 9/11, and sold to eBay for $1.5 billion. The book’s thesis is that the famous later “PayPal Mafia” (YouTube, Yelp, Tesla, SpaceX, LinkedIn, Palantir, and more) is poorly understood without the four-year near-failure origin story: PalmPilot beaming, email money, eBay network effects, IGOR fraud tools, board coups, and regulatory gauntlets. Chess-themed part titles (Sicilian Defense; Bad Bishop; Doubled Rooks) frame the competitive, adversarial culture.
For this United States 1990–present wiki the source is central to post–Cold War Silicon Valley fintech, eBay’s payments politics, early CAPTCHA/fraud engineering, founder-board power fights, and the alumni network that remade tech after the IPO. EPUB structure: Dedication; epigraphs (Machiavelli, Ada Lovelace); Introduction; three titled parts totaling twenty-two numbered chapters; Epilogue; photo captions; Debts (acknowledgments); A Note on Sources and Methods; About the Author; Also by; Notes; Copyright. (Notes TOC also lists “Conclusion: The Floor,” which does not appear as a separate body chapter in this pandoc extract—the closing narrative is the Epilogue.)
Narrative Source Flow
Introduction
Lines 47–401. January 2019 living-room interview: Musk “rummages around the attic” on PayPal while Tesla/SpaceX layoffs swirl. PayPal alumni as a controversial power network—“PayPal Mafia”—spanning YouTube, Yelp, Tesla, SpaceX, LinkedIn, Palantir, VC, nonprofits, and politics; admirers vs critics of techno-libertarian influence. Origin thesis: Confinity (Fieldlink) and X.com converge on email payments and eBay; merger, fraud, lawsuits, Billpoint war, post-9/11 IPO, then $1.5B eBay sale. Method note: hundreds of interviews, emails, board minutes, Weekly Pal newsletters; aim to restore the glossed-over founding years before later myths.
Part 1 — Sicilian Defense
Ch. 1 — Building Blocks
Lines 406–1042. Max Levchin origin: Chernobyl fallout near Pripyat; mother’s radiology-lab computers (DVK-2 / Robotron) and Pascal; Jewish family under Soviet pressure; 1991 Chicago immigration; UIUC ACM culture; Luke Nosek and Scott Banister; libertarian reading and early start-up attempts. Building blocks for the engineer who will become PayPal’s CTO and fraud-fighter.
Ch. 2 — The Pitch
Lines 1043–1569. Peter Thiel path: Stanford / Stanford Review contrarianism; Supreme Court clerkship rejection; Credit Suisse then Thiel Capital with Ken Howery; Levchin–Thiel Hobee’s pitch meetings and brain-teaser culture; John Powers joins; Fieldlink as mobile-security / “field” cryptography startup. Seed of Confinity’s founding trio and puzzle-driven hiring.
Ch. 3 — The Right Questions
Lines 1570–2071. Elon Musk finance apprenticeship: Bank of Nova Scotia internship under Peter Nicholson; Brady Bonds / Latin American debt project and banks’ refusal to innovate; Queen’s → Penn → Silicon Valley; Zip2 with Kimbal (city guides, VC, sale-era frustration). Closes the pre-X.com arc: Zip2 wealth and Musk’s resolve to rebuild finance from first principles.
Ch. 4 — “What Matters to Me Is Winning”
Lines 2072–2676. X.com founding vision: “Amazon of financial services”—accounts, trading, credit, insurance on ancient bank mainframes’ ruins; Harris Fricker and Christopher Payne cofounders; purchase of the x.com domain; Musk’s large personal capital stake and wariness of Zip2-style investor control. Ambition and early team-building before products exist.
Ch. 5 — The Beamers
Lines 2677–3428. Fieldlink needs a CEO: Thiel as “ramp-up CEO”; hiring UIUC classmates Yu Pan and Russel Simmons; office culture at 394 University; product pivot from Palm security toward money beaming; Confinity rename and Nokia Ventures path. The “beamers” era that puts Confinity on the map.
Ch. 6 — Hosed
Lines 3429–4172. Neighbors at 394 University: Confinity vs X.com mutual disdain; Beaming at Buck’s (July 23, 1999) Nokia $4.5M PalmPilot demo after sleepless compiles; naming PayPal with Master-McNeil; email-payments pivot; growth, server crises, and “hosed” engineering culture as both firms race.
Ch. 7 — Money Talks
Lines 4173–4764. X.com hollowed after Fricker-era departures; Scott Alexander hire (“money talks”); Sequoia’s Michael Moritz and “happy gas” VC climate; product launch, viral bonuses, and security-flaw New York Times storm. Closes Part 1 with X.com as a real, messy online bank/payments contender.
Part 2 — Bad Bishop
Ch. 8 — If You Build It
Lines 4769–5606. Post-launch deluge: Mick E. Mouse accounts, checkbook spam, “the cave” call center; January 2000 security-flaw media crisis; Confinity/X.com scale pain as eBay sellers adopt email pay. Building it invites the customers—and the fraudsters—who redefine the company.
Ch. 9 — The Widget Wars
Lines 5607–6106. Confinity vs X.com battle for eBay: dumpster-diving paranoia, Thiel signup on Musk’s screen, 20 vs 10 referral wars, scrapers and auction widgets; network-effects thesis. Ends in merger logic—fight is destroying both—setting up Crash.
Ch. 10 — Crash
Lines 6107–6642. Musk’s McLaren F1 Sand Hill Road crash with Thiel en route to Sequoia merger talks; Bill Harris as joint CEO experiment; due diligence red flags, burn rate, culture clash, and Billpoint/eBay threat. Merger closes under crisis, not calm.
Ch. 11 — The Nut House Coup
Lines 6643–7414. Customer-service meltdown (tens of thousands of calls; Wallace’s 100k email backlog); Omaha operations seed; Antonio’s Nut House bar meeting; Sacks/Musk alignment against Bill Harris; Harris ousted—“Nut House Coup”—and Musk reinstated as CEO with Thiel as chairman. Founder power reasserts after professional-CEO failure.
Ch. 12 — Buttoned-Up
Lines 7415–8279. Musk’s June 2000 reorg: Sacks on product, Hoffman on BD/international, Levchin as CTO; small agile-ish producer/engineer pods (Hurley/Pan auction work); Mythical Man-Month lessons; V2 platform fights and X-PayPal branding tension. Attempts to professionalize without killing speed.
Ch. 13 — The Sword
Lines 8280–8950. Roelof Botha joins (brain teaser; Meg Whitman “sword of Damocles” over eBay dependency); spreadsheet runway models; fraud and fee hemorrhage; push toward sustainability as markets crack. Finance discipline arrives as the hangman’s sword becomes visible.
Ch. 14 — Ambition’s Debt
Lines 8951–9524. Musk honeymoon/Olympics trip (Sept 2000) as cover for vote-of-no-confidence; Levchin/Thiel/Nosek/Banister coup vs V2 and brand change; board sides with mutineers; Thiel interim CEO (Sept 24–28 arc); Musk remains large shareholder. Ouster as the debt of founder ambition—and the hinge into Part 3.
Part 3 — Doubled Rooks
Ch. 15 — Igor
Lines 9529–10260. Fake CEO search while Thiel stays; David Solo almost-hire who endorses Thiel; fraud typology (merchant vs professional rings); Gausebeck-Levchin CAPTCHA as early commercial bot test; IGOR system named for fraudster “Igor”; random-deposit verification. Fraud engineering as survival, not side quest.
Ch. 16 — Use the Force
Lines 10261–10730. Revenue: Business/Premier upsell and forced upgrades; “PayPal Paul” Martin on auction boards; walking the tightrope after abandoning “always free.” Product and community force as twin levers—and user fury as cost of monetization.
Ch. 17 — Crime in Progress
Lines 10731–11198. FBI Operation Flyhook (Gorshkov/Ivanov); Russian hackers’ PayPal/eBay fraud factories; domestic fraud rings and “Greg Stivenson”; law-enforcement alliance and stigma of being crime infrastructure. Crime-in-progress framing for why IGOR and partnerships matter.
Ch. 18 — Guerrillas
Lines 11199–11826. Billpoint/Visa free-fee “declaration of war”; Sacks’s eBay Response Team; message-board guerrillas, PR, legal nastygrams; Hoffman’s eBay diplomacy. Guerrilla warfare for auction share while forced upgrades make PayPal vulnerable.
Ch. 19 — World Domination
Lines 11827–12397. World Domination Index / New World Currency rhetoric; UK/Europe/euro expansion; international fundraising; regulatory thickets abroad. Ambition to be borderless money meets banking law reality.
Ch. 20 — Blindsided
Lines 12398–13023. Dot-com wreckage (Pets.com); Thiel’s August 2001 profitability push (blue-hair bet; snack fees; Ishii badge-store); IPO rationale and SEC gauntlet prep. Markets and regulators blindside the “thermonuclear IPO” dream—discipline becomes the product.
Ch. 21 — Outlaws
Lines 13024–13715. Post-9/11 S-1 filing (seventeen days after); CertCo and other IPO-window lawsuits; hostile SEC examiner lore; February 15, 2002 Nasdaq debut (PYPL); Thiel parking-lot speed-chess spectacle. Outlaw posture—shipping through catastrophe—nearly scuttles then crowns the IPO.
Ch. 22 — And All I Got Was a T-Shirt
Lines 13716–15238. Lock-up wealth watching; Billpoint/Wells Fargo threat; eBay “Orca/Ernie” talks; T-shirt raid at eBay live event; July 8, 2002 acquisition news (~$1.5B); sumo-suit last day; alumni lessons (hire non-payments people; immigrants as entrepreneurs; last-job-as-employee culture). Independence ends; the network begins.
Epilogue
Lines 15239–15743. “PayPal Mafia” as media phrase—useful and distorting; global copycat “mafias.” Extended coda: Chris Wilson and Stephen Edwards at Patuxent prison study the Fortune Mafia photo, preach founder networks to inmates, and treat the story as an “easy preach” of agency. Photo-caption block (Levchin high school through IPO chess, eBay T-shirts, Fortune cover) closes the narrative apparatus before Debts.
Debts / Sources note / About the Author / Notes / Copyright
Lines 15744–16241. Debts (acknowledgments: Alice Mayhew, Stephanie Frerich, interviewees, Ashlee Vance, Walter Isaacson, et al.); A Note on Sources and Methods (archive.org, Weekly Pal, 200+ interviews, fact-checking, narrative-fallacy caveat); About the Author; Also by; Notes (part/chapter cue list including “Conclusion: The Floor”); Copyright (ISBN 978-1-5011-9726-0; ebook 978-1-5011-9725-3; First Simon & Schuster hardcover edition February 2022).

IPO and regulation

sources/stone-everything-store.content:
The Everything Store
Author: Brad Stone
Published: 2013 (Little, Brown and Company; First ebook edition October 2013)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash 0e1d9a8e3164e864123fc866961855d5)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/stone-everything-store.txt (pandoc plain from EPUB)
Extract stats: 12,688 lines · ~118,012 words · 729,667 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
HOME wiki is United States 1990–present. Bezos childhood / Vanguard / ranch years (Prologue framing and Ch. 5) are prologue for the 1994–2013 Amazon arc that sits inside the period. No sister-period copy required for 1946–89 unless a future mining pass wants Houston gifted-education or New Mexico ranch context alone.
Overview
The Everything Store is Stone’s reported company biography of Amazon and Jeff Bezos: Wall Street quant apprenticeship at D. E. Shaw; the 1994 Seattle bookstore bet and “Get Big Fast” expansion; survival and first profits through the dot-com bust; internal reorganizations (two-pizza teams, frugality rituals); the turn toward AWS and Kindle as proof Amazon was a technology company; then post-recession retail conquest, Zappos/Diapers battles, and the public controversies over sales tax, publishers, and pricing. The book opens on “Tim” in Houston’s Vanguard program, then frames Bezos as a Jobs-like micromanager whose customer gospel coexists with scorched-earth competition. Stone draws on 300+ interviews; Bezos judged a reflective book “too early” but approved many interviews with executives, family, and friends.
For this United States 1990–present wiki the source is central to internet retail after the Web boom, Seattle as a tech capital, platform Marketplace and cloud infrastructure, the e-book disruption of publishers and bookstores, and the public fight over whether Amazon is missionary or mercenary. EPUB structure: Dedication; Epigraph (Princeton commencement); Prologue; three Parts (Faith; Literary Influences; Missionary or Mercenary?) with eleven numbered chapters; Photos; Acknowledgments; Appendix (Jeff’s Reading List); Notes; About the Author; Newsletters; Copyright.
Narrative Source Flow
Prologue
Lines 34–430. Julie Ray’s 1970s Vanguard visit and the pseudonymous sixth-grader “Tim” (infinity cube, teacher survey, productive-thinking circle); Stone tracks Ray decades later and reveals Tim as Bezos. Portrait of Bezos’s laugh, door-desks, six-page narratives instead of PowerPoint, reality-distortion field, and competitive damage to Circuit City / Borders / Best Buy / Barnes & Noble. Reporting method: 300+ interviews, Bezos cooperation with the “too early” caveat; thesis of a gifted child who bets on the Internet and a single store that sells everything.
PART I — Faith
Line 431. Frame for founding through bust survival.
Ch. 1 — The House of Quants
Lines 435–887. D. E. Shaw as quant lab; Bezos as rising deputy researching Internet commerce; MacKenzie and the “regret minimization” cross-country move; Cadabra / Amazon naming; early Seattle garage and recruiting Nick Hanauer, Shel Kaphan, and others; do-not-poach clock with Shaw; Holden call—“It’s time. This is going to work.”
Ch. 2 — The Book of Bezos
Lines 888–2149. Usenet hiring post; Relentless.com kept as redirect; Bellevue ranch house; books as first category for selection and distributor logistics; garage-to-Columbia Building scramble; venture capital and “Get Big Fast”; May 1997 IPO and Barnes & Noble lawsuit; early employees displaced as Bezos installs a more experienced cohort; Shel Kaphan as loyal early parent who learns Amazon has only one true parent.
Ch. 3 — Fever Dreams
Lines 2150–3425. 1997 Harvard Business School session where students urge sale to Barnes & Noble; category expansion, Toys “R” Us and other partnerships, Junglee and other acquisitions; international bets; fulfillment chaos and holiday near-meltdowns; stock-market exuberance and billion-dollar loss trajectory into 2000 as the fever breaks.
Ch. 4 — Milliravi
Lines 3426–4737. Dot-com bust, Barron’s “Amazon.bomb,” and stock collapse; cash raises and “Get Our House in Order”; Marketplace / third-party sellers and publisher/Authors Guild anger; Amabot vs. handcrafted editorial; Amazon Prime’s free-shipping flywheel; first profitable quarter (Jan 2002) and the press-release Easter egg milliravi aimed at analyst Ravi Suria—“They had won.”
PART II — Literary Influences
Line 4738. Frame for biography, culture books, and product inventions that remake Amazon’s identity.
Ch. 5 — Rocket Boy
Lines 4742–5478. Competitive streak traced to childhood: Ted Jorgensen (biological father), Jackie and adoptive father Mike Bezos, Pop Gise’s ranch and “harder to be kind than clever”; Miami Palmetto High, Princeton, Wall Street path. Parallel Bezos project Blue Origin and space ambition as literary/engineering influence alongside Amazon’s reading-list culture.
Ch. 6 — Chaos Theory
Lines 5479–6679. Post-profitability growth into new categories and countries; fulfillment-center disorder (knives on conveyors, hardcover/paperback prompts for toys); S-Team, metrics, and two-pizza teams; bureaucracy hunters (TV / Door-Desk awards); end of one-on-ones with Bezos; Coffeyville squatter vignette as warehouse surrealism.
Ch. 7 — A Technology Company, Not a Retailer
Lines 6680–7760. Tenth-anniversary Benaroya Hall gala (Dylan/Norah Jones livestreamed); Google era makes Amazon look like a thin-margin retailer; search defections and Bezos nutters; AWS conceived from internal need and Creation / Innovator’s Dilemma thinking; cloud services enlarge “everything store” into infrastructure—Amazon finally reads as the tech company Bezos claimed.
Ch. 8 — Fiona
Lines 7761–8952. Rocketbook / NuvoMedia prologue; code name Fiona and Lab126; obsessive Kindle development, Whispernet, and Nov 2007 W Hotel launch as Gutenberg challenge; Barnes & Noble’s Riggio disbelief as tactical blunder; publishers squeezed; Fiona as hinge into a phase of innovation plus ruthless ecosystem control.
PART III — Missionary or Mercenary?
Line 8953. Frame for post-2007 scale, controversy, and unfinished everything-company ambition.
Ch. 9 — Liftoff!
Lines 8957–9822. Phoenix 3 fulfillment center as physical everything store; 2007+ sales acceleration and third-party surge; recession as gift that weakens big-box rivals; Zappos pursuit and ~$900M equity deal; Diapers.com / Quidsi pressure; Kindle and AWS lift Amazon into the same breath as Google and Apple—“high orbit.”
Ch. 10 — Expedient Convictions
Lines 9823–11038. 2010–11 scrutiny: sales-tax avoidance, acquisition mechanics, Amazon Publishing vs. suppliers, MAP / “hide the price” workarounds. Bezos’s “willingness to be misunderstood” and Doerr/Komisar missionary-vs-mercenary rhetoric as rhetorical jujitsu; expedient convictions that also serve strategic interests.
Ch. 11 — The Kingdom of the Question Mark
Lines 11039–~11822. Near-twentieth-anniversary everything store (Marketplace + AWS + new categories); Roadrunner Bike Center / Ted Jorgensen as polar opposite of Amazon scale; Day 1 inventiveness anxiety and failed “personal voice” email experiments; close on missionary and mercenary as a potent combination, still weaving a rope of small advantages until Bezos exits or no one stands in the way. Photo captions follow in extract before apparatus.
Acknowledgments / Appendix / Notes / Copyright
Lines 11957–12688. Acknowledgments (Little, Brown team; Amazon PR and executives; journalists including Ashlee Vance); Appendix — Jeff’s Reading List (Remains of the Day, Walton, Mythical Man-Month, Collins, Christensen, Goldratt, Taleb, etc.); Notes from Prologue through Ch. 11; trailing TOC echo; Copyright © 2013 by Brad Stone; Little, Brown / Hachette; ISBN 978-0-316-21925-9; First ebook edition October 2013.
Coverage Guide
Internet retail founding and Get Big Fast
Chs. 1–3 for D. E. Shaw → Seattle bookstore → IPO → category fever—core period entrepreneurship narrative.
Dot-com bust survival
Ch. 4 for cash, Marketplace, Prime, Amabot, and first profits / milliravi.
Bezos biography and Blue Origin side quest
Ch. 5 (and Prologue) for origin story and space parallel; mine lightly for pre-1990 detail.
Operating system: teams, frugality, warehouses
Ch. 6 for two-pizza teams, Door-Desk culture, and fulfillment chaos.
AWS and Kindle as tech proof
Chs. 7–8 for cloud and e-reader as identity shift.
Post-recession conquest and public controversy
Chs. 9–10 for Zappos/Quidsi, Prime-era retail war, tax/publishing/MAP fights.
Everything-company unfinished arc
Ch. 11 for 2012–13 scale and missionary/mercenary close.

Call Me Ted
Author: Ted Turner with Bill Burke
Published: 2008 (Grand Central Publishing / Hachette; first eBook November 2008)
Working text: Digital EPUB via Anna’s Archive (hash b2b0ddf22332740fd82dbd1e2f87e8c9)
Raw extract: wiki/raw/turner-call-me-ted.txt (EPUB via pandoc -t plain)
Extract stats: 12,954 lines · ~134,427 words · 751,108 bytes
Deploy note: Full-text raw is not deployed — wiki/.gitignore ignores *.txt; Quartz ignorePatterns includes raw.
Period-Overlap Note
This source has been copied from United States 1946-89 into the United States 1990–present wiki because Chapters 24–33 + Appendix cover CNN under Tom Johnson and the Gulf War, Cartoon Network/TNT strategy, network merger feelers, the Time Warner combination, the UN Foundation billion-dollar pledge, the AOL deal that diluted Turner’s power, September 11 from CNN Center, and stepping away into philanthropy—core post–Cold War media-consolidation material. Mine those chapters first. Chapters 4–23 (billboards through SuperStation/CNN founding, MGM, cable rescue, Jane Fonda/land) belong primarily to 1946–89; use only as brief continuity. Chs. 1–3 childhood are background only.
Overview
Call Me Ted is Robert Edward “Ted” Turner III’s first-person life of media entrepreneurship and competitive sailing, written with Bill Burke. For this United States 1990–present wiki the usable core is the post–Berlin Wall arc: CNN’s Gulf War legitimacy, entertainment-network expansion under Time Warner constraints, the 1995–96 merger into Time Warner, the UN billion pledge, and the 2000 AOL combination that phased him out. Period-gate hard on pre-1990 founding chapters except as continuity.
EPUB structure: copyright/Contents; dedication; Preface; Chapters 1–33; Appendix (Eleven Voluntary Initiatives); Acknowledgments; photo credits.
Narrative Source Flow
Front matter / Contents / dedication
Lines 1–111. © 2008 Turner Works, LLC; Grand Central / Hachette imprint; ISBN 978-0-446-54336-1; Contents listing Preface through Acknowledgments; dedication to Turner’s children.
Preface
Lines 112–156. Why write now after stepping away; setbacks (father and sister, sailing near-death, Braves losing years, later wealth loss); philanthropy and five children; invitation to the ride.
Chapter 1 — Early Years
Lines 157–492. Birth 19 November 1938, Cincinnati; Ed Turner and Florence Rooney; sister Mary Jean (1941); father’s Navy service and four-year-old boarding school; postwar family moves; early nature passion and difficult father.
Chapter 2 — McCallie
Lines 493–907. Seventh-grade boarding at McCallie military academy, Chattanooga; youngest boarder; discipline, demerits, and competitive drive; father’s purse-string control of schooling.
Chapter 3 — College and the Coast Guard
Lines 908–1528. Senior-year college choice; Brown University; mischief with Peter Dames; Coast Guard service; father’s insistence on eventual takeover of the billboard company.
Chapter 4 — Billboards
Lines 1529–1913. Post-college Florida rebellion with Dames; return into Turner Advertising; learning outdoor sales and plant operations under Ed Turner’s expansion in the South.
Chapter 5 — Tragedy
Lines 1914–2094. Summer 1962 General Outdoor deal with Bob Naegele to make Turner the South’s largest billboard operator; father’s mounting stress and erratic behavior; suicide (gunshot), March 1963.
Chapter 6 — Picking Up the Pieces
Lines 2095–2320. Jimmy Brown first on the scene; warning signs and $50,000 check to stepmother Jane; holding the company together amid debt and competitor pressure.
Chapter 7 — On My Own
Lines 2321–2667. By end of March 1963 Turner as chairman/president; son Robert Edward Turner IV born May 1963; marriage to Judy failing; consolidating control of the billboard business.
Chapter 8 — Sailing Gets Serious
Lines 2668–3038. Mid-1960s sailing intensity alongside business; Flying Dutchman and yacht-club life; Ferrari anecdote; racing ladder that later leads to ocean racing and the Cup.
Chapter 9 — WTCG: “Watch This Channel Grow!”
Lines 3039–3619. Late-1960s radio holdings without Atlanta 24-hour outlet; billboard ad for UHF WJRJ Channel 17; purchase and rebranding push; movies, wrestling, counterprogramming against network affiliates.
Chapter 10 — The Braves
Lines 3620–4161. Braves telecasts as ratings and UHF-receiver catalyst (~100,000 estimated new converters); ballpark enthusiasm amid losing seasons; path toward franchise ownership to secure rights and identity.
Chapter 11 — The SuperStation
Lines 4162–4763. Growth ceiling in Atlanta vs. Big Three affiliates; satellite distribution leap—WTCG as national cable SuperStation; “bigger footprint” strategy and operator relationships.
Chapter 12 — The America’s Cup
Lines 4764–5212. Competitive sailing peak around SuperStation launch; campaign toward and winning the 1977 America’s Cup; “Captain Outrageous” public persona alongside media expansion.
Chapter 13 — Cable News Network
Lines 5213–5526. Cable partnership creed (“you run the wires, I’ll make them sing”—Bob Magness/TCI); 1978 decision to launch all-news channel himself after years of no one else doing it; naming and early planning for CNN.
Chapter 14 — Fastnet
Lines 5527–5872. 1979 Fastnet Race ordeal while CNN preparations advance; near-disaster at sea; return to intensify the nine-months-to-launch countdown.
Chapter 15 — CNN Launch
Lines 5873–6200. Country-club facility retrofit; Reese Schonfeld / Burt Reinhardt hiring surge; launching without enough capital to reach profitability; race against copycats and lenders’ skepticism.
Chapter 16 — A Dagger Pointed at Our Heart
Lines 6201–6661. 1980 America’s Cup defense attempt with Courageous vs. Dennis Conner while CNN is newborn; competitive and financial strain; “dagger” metaphor for threats to the young news network.
Chapter 17 — World Citizen
Lines 6662–6905. International travel and Cold War–era public diplomacy instincts; using media reach and sports for global visibility beyond U.S. cable homes.
Chapter 18 — The Goodwill Games
Lines 6906–7118. Post-Olympic-boycott alternative: Goodwill Games concept and Moscow staging; sports diplomacy brand alongside CNN’s international ambitions.
Chapter 19 — CBS
Lines 7119–7538. Mid-1980s scale logic—own broadcast network plus cable; exploratory pursuit of CBS; Big Three slow to enter cable; failed/blocked path that pushes other expansion routes.
Chapter 20 — MGM
Lines 7539–7903. Studio merger talks with Kirk Kerkorian / MGM-UA to secure film library against Hollywood leverage; purchase and debt load that reshape Turner’s balance sheet.
Chapter 21 — The Cable Operators
Lines 7904–8198. John Malone / TCI rescue and cable MSO equity alliance after MGM strain; shared fight against broadcast networks; accepting outside ownership to keep assets in the cable camp.
Chapter 22 — Meeting Jane Fonda
Lines 8199–8492. Courtship and marriage to Jane Fonda; public/political celebrity intersection with Turner’s media persona.
Chapter 23 — “Give Me Land, Lots of Land”
Lines 8493–8694. Montana Bar None then Flying D Ranch (~119,000 acres); bison pasture vision; land conservation turn that prefigures later philanthropy.
Chapter 24 — The Gulf War
Lines 8695–9058. Tom Johnson hired to lead CNN (1990); Gulf War coverage cementing CNN’s global news role—wiki core for this period.
Chapter 25 — Movies and Cartoons
Lines 9059–9466. 1990s strategy: own programming; TNT success; Cartoon Network and library exploitation under Time Warner board constraints.
Chapter 26 — Networking
Lines 9467–9857. Continued ABC/NBC/CBS merger feelers; Cap Cities/ABC Olympics talks; Jerry Levin blocking network purchase.
Chapter 27 — Time Warner Merger
Lines 9858–10188. Summer 1995: O.J. ratings spike; agreement to merge Turner into Time Warner.
Chapter 28 — The New Time Warner
Lines 10189–10674. Post-announcement Braves World Series 1995; integration politics inside the combined company.
Chapter 29 — Billion-Dollar Gift
Lines 10675–11023. Philanthropy seminar roots; $1 billion pledge to UN causes / UN Foundation.
Chapter 30 — Transitions
Lines 11024–11377. Jonathan Levin murder; personal and corporate transitions around the UN Foundation decision.
Chapter 31 — AOL: Phased Out and Fenced In
Lines 11378–11866. January 2000 AOL–Time Warner deal whirlwind; divorce from Jane same week; dilution and loss of influence.
Chapter 32 — Stepping Away
Lines 11867–12370. September 11 from CNN Center; final exit from corporate power.
Chapter 33 — Onward and Upward
Lines 12371–12864. Post-business focus on global problems, conservation, and energy; closing creed.
Appendix — Eleven Voluntary Initiatives
Lines 12865–12916. Pocket list of personal pledges (planet, weapons, UN, renewable energy/climate added 2008).
Acknowledgments
Lines 12917–12954. Mort Janklow; Hachette team; Debbie Masterson, Taylor Glover; Elizabeth Dewberry; Bill Burke; photo credits.
Coverage Guide
Founding media empire (continuity ← 1946–89)
