Period-Overlap Note
HOME wiki is United States 1990–present. The book’s core action (post–Cold War military space frustration → PhoneSat/Planet → Rocket Lab Electron → Astra → Firefly) sits squarely inside the period. New Zealand childhood/shed years for Peter Beck and Ukraine/Belarus backstories for Max Polyakov and Artiom Anisimov are origin prologue for U.S.-facing New Space companies, customers, and regulators. No sister-period copy required unless a future mining pass wants pre-1990 rocket-pioneer epigraph context alone.
Overview
When the Heavens Went on Sale is Vance’s five-year, multi-continent immersion in the New Space / smallsat launch boom that follows SpaceX’s proof that private rocketry can work. The book is explicitly not a SpaceX biography: Falcon 1 on Kwajalein opens as prologue myth, then the narrative tracks Planet Labs’ Earth-imaging constellation; Rocket Lab and Peter Beck’s Electron; Chris Kemp’s Stealth→Astra grind toward daily small launches; and Tom Markusic / Max Polyakov’s Firefly drama under U.S. national-security pressure. Framing thesis: low Earth orbit as a coming “computing shell” / mass-transit highway, powered by a shared hallucination of founders, welders, DARPA, and SPACs.
For this United States 1990–present wiki the source is central to post-Shuttle commercial space, Silicon Valley hardware culture at NASA Ames, Pentagon “responsive space,” venture-funded rocketry, and the politics of foreign capital in U.S. launch. EPUB structure: Dedication; Preface; Prologue; four titled parts (The Great Computer in the Sky; The Peter Beck Project; Ad Astra; The Maddest Max) totaling thirty-three numbered chapters; Epilogue; Thanks and Acknowledgments; Index; Photo Section; About the Author; Also by; Copyright; About the Publisher.
Narrative Source Flow
Prologue — A Shared Hallucination
Lines 143–849. September 2008 Falcon 1 success on Kwajalein as the door-opening myth; Musk/Bezos as billionaire unlockers; then the wider New Space cast—Planet, Rocket Lab/Electron, and a swarm of underfunded small-rocket hopefuls—betting that frequent cheap rides change the LEO economy from scarce railways to mass transit. Thesis close: space as shared hallucination, mythology plus capitalism, with Pete Worden as early military catalyst and comedy/tragedy ahead for the main companies.
Part: The Great Computer in the Sky (Planet Labs)
Ch. 1 — When Doves Fly
Lines 850–1187. February 2017 Chennai: Robbie Schingler and Planet Labs’ record 104-satellite PSLV ride (eighty-eight Planet “Doves”); constellation thesis—cheap shoebox cameras photographing the whole Earth daily and selling imagery as an online service; company survival stakes and national-pride Indian launch framing.
Ch. 2 — Space Force
Lines 1188–1375. Brigadier General Simon “Pete” Worden: Office of Strategic Influence fiasco after 9/11; Defense/DARPA frustration with Boeing–Lockheed launch scarcity; early SpaceX Falcon 1 contract and Kwajalein oversight; “responsive space” agenda that seeds later smallsat/small-rocket demand.
Ch. 3 — Welcome, Lord Vader
Lines 1376–2402. Worden takes NASA Ames; Silicon Valley’s uncelebrated past vs Ames as temple; PhoneSat and DIY satellite culture; “Pete’s Kids” attract Will Marshall, Robbie Schingler, Chris Kemp, and allied misfits into the Ames orbit that will birth Planet and later Astra connections.
Ch. 4 — The Rainbow Mansion
Lines 2403–2737. 2006 Cupertino commune at 21677 Rainbow Drive: Marshall, Schingler, Jessy Kate Cowan-Sharp, Kemp, and others invent communal living next to Ames; Rainbow Mansion as incubator salon for PhoneSat ideas and the future Planet Labs founding circle.
Ch. 5 — Phoning Home
Lines 2738–3267. Will Marshall’s English countryside childhood, risk philosophy, nature/conservation bent; path into NASA Ames science and the PhoneSat project with Chris Boshuizen—consumer phones as satellite guts.
Ch. 6 — The Birth of a Planet
Lines 3268–3793. Spreadsheet ranking of smallsat missions at the Rainbow Mansion; imagery wins; Planet Labs founding logic—many cheap short-lived cameras vs few billion-dollar buses; Cosmogia / Planet brand and the bid to democratize Earth observation.
Ch. 7 — The Great Computer in the Sky
Lines 3794–4560. Payoff chapter: Planet imagery in open-source intelligence (Decker Eveleth and Chinese missile-silo hunt, 2021); daily global record as geopolitical and commercial infrastructure; closes the Planet arc as “great computer in the sky.”
Part: The Peter Beck Project (Rocket Lab)
Ch. 8 — Big, If True
Lines 4561–4904. Vance in Auckland 2018; awkward Musk phone call (post–Elon Musk biography chill) while reporting Rocket Lab; Beck introduced as the other private company regularly orbiting satellites for customers.
Ch. 9 — A Boy and His Shed
Lines 4905–5255. Peter Beck childhood in Invercargill, gearhead New Zealand, Burt Munro lore; shed tinkerer origin myth for the future Electron founder.
Ch. 10 — You Just Stick It Between Your Legs and Pray
Lines 5256–5573. Number 8 wire mentality vs Beck’s ambition; Fisher & Paykel years and extreme DIY engineering that foreshadows Rocket Lab methods.
Ch. 11 — I Expected More from You, America
Lines 5574–5899. Yacht titanium-doorknob absurdity; Industrial Research Limited (IRL) Auckland; Beck’s U.S. contacts and disappointment with American aerospace bureaucracy; decision path toward building a Kiwi rocket company.
Ch. 12 — “You Fucking Beauty!”
Lines 5900–6439. Sounding rockets first; Rocket Lab founding; Ātea-1 and the ecstatic first reaches-space moment; Mark Rocket early money and the shoestring company that almost nobody notices.
Ch. 13 — The Military Is Not So Bad
Lines 6440–6783. Silicon Valley ignores Beck; DARPA/U.S. military does not—responsive-space interest in Ātea tech, propellants, and composite lightness; defense contracts keep Rocket Lab alive.
Ch. 14 — Enter Electron
Lines 6784–7602. 2013 California fundraising grind ($5M ask after a painful earlier dilution); pitch that tens of thousands of smallsats need frequent launch; Electron design, Mahia launch site, carbon-fiber vehicle; path from skepticism to orbital success.
Ch. 15 — You’ve Got Our Attention
Lines 7603–8225. 2018 unicorn raise (~140M; >1B valuation); Darth Vader HQ aesthetics; industrial Electron factory; Rocket Lab as SpaceX’s smallsat-frequency counterpart and competitive pressure on later Astra chapters.
Part: Ad Astra (Astra / Chris Kemp)
Ch. 16 — Let’s Make a Lot of Fucking Rockets
Lines 8226–8818. Rumors of SoMa rocket maker Ventions / Adam London; DoD/DARPA tiny-rocket contracts; Chris Kemp’s Stealth Space rebirth of the Ventions tech toward daily cheap launch from Alameda.
Ch. 17 — Chris Kemp on Chris Kemp, Spring 2017
Lines 8819–9200. Method chapter: long first-person Kemp monologue (Alabama childhood, Space Camp, start-up résumé, Nebula lessons); Vance’s “hear them talk” immersion contract for the Astra arc.
Ch. 18 — The Grind
Lines 9201–9745. Alameda former navy base; aluminum simplicity vs Rocket Lab carbon fiber; five hand-built engines; city-regulation skirmishes; countdown-clock culture of building a rocket in a year.
Ch. 19 — Party Like You Mean It
Lines 9746–9943. Stealth Space renames to Astra (Oct 2017); recruiters and suppliers force the rebrand; factory party celebrating a whole rocket on the floor.
Ch. 20 — Your Friendly Neighborhood Fog Monster
Lines 9944–10223. First upright outdoor tests; Chris Thompson (ex-SpaceX) joins; fog/noise over Orion Street; neighbors, Pottery Barn Outlet, and the ICBM-in-the-backyard vibe.
Ch. 21 — Not-So-Stealth Space
Lines 10224–10556. Factory expansion and Alaska first-flight plan; iterate-don’t-perfect philosophy; Ventions tech as head start; tension between software-speed culture and aerospace risk.
Ch. 22 — Northern Exposure
Lines 10557–11182. Kodiak / Pacific Spaceport Complex campaign; Rocket 1 launch attempt atmosphere (including Vance’s stripper-plane digression); Alaska as Astra’s proving ground.
Ch. 23 — Rocket 2
Lines 11183–11817. Sparse data from Rocket 1; Kemp’s optimistic investor spin; Rocket Lab orbital pressure and temporary Electron snag; Frankenmachine vs polished Electron race.
Ch. 24 — It’s a Job
Lines 11818–12096. RV park outside the Alameda factory; Les Martin, Matthew Flanagan, and cynical gearhead labor culture; Bay Area housing costs as aerospace subplot.
Ch. 25 — The Reset Button
Lines 12097–12608. Commercial rocket failure psychology vs government programs; explosions as deflation of founder exceptionalism; Astra reset after catastrophic attempts.
Ch. 26 — Cash on Fire
Lines 12609–12857. Rocket 3 / mobile-launcher destruction; helium mishap lore; COVID supply and LOX shortages; Pentagon “essential” designation; cash burn while still unproven.
Ch. 27 — It Makes Sense. Right?
Lines 12858–13229. February 2021 Astra SPAC / Nasdaq listing in the covid SPAC bubble; Wall Street hype vs launch reality; Kemp’s public-markets bet closing the Astra narrative arc.
Part: The Maddest Max (Firefly)
Ch. 28 — On Passion
Lines 13230–13490. Max Polyakov at the Texas Beer Barn; ~$200M personal plunge into Firefly Aerospace; Cedar Park / Firefly Farm introduction; Ukrainian-Silicon Valley odd-couple energy with Tom Markusic.
Ch. 29 — God Told Me to Do It
Lines 13491–14210. Tom Markusic origin: Mantua, Ohio; farm/machine “essence of engineering”; NASA/SpaceX/Blue Origin résumé; religious mission framing and Firefly’s first life/death spiral before Polyakov money.
Ch. 30 — Full Attack
Lines 14211–14946. Artiom Anisimov (Belarus→space law→Polyakov orbit); rescue/rebuild of Firefly; Ukraine industrial ties; full-attack capitalization and governance after near-collapse.
Ch. 31 — These Rockets: They’re Expensive
Lines 14947–15394. Menlo Park mansion / Oktoberfest; burn rate and investor theater; Vandenberg path; cost reality of trying to be the next orbital small-launcher.
Ch. 32 — Limits
Lines 15395–15593. Engine-test barbecue and Polyakov’s rage at missed deadlines; founder–workforce collision; limits of passion capital and schedule optimism.
Ch. 33 — Flameout
Lines 15594–15877. December 2020: Treasury/Air Force/NASA pressure; Polyakov forced off board and toward selling control as Firefly nears Vandenberg launch; badge downgraded to “Escort only”; national-security politics as flameout of the odd couple’s governance.
Epilogue
Lines 15878–16324. LeoLabs as commercial LEO “air traffic control”; Starlink/OneWeb/Planet debris and collision alerts; SpaceX dominance restated; SPAC hangover and 2022 risk-off markets. Character updates: Polyakov pushed out then watching Firefly’s successful second launch from afar; Markusic later ousted by professional investors; Polyakov’s Ukraine-war imagery pipeline; Planet/Rocket Lab/Astra/Firefly futures under competitive and capital pressure; closing “look up” return to the Alan Moore epigraph.

Period-Overlap Note
HOME wiki is United States 1990–present. Childhood Kentucky / Oneida (Ch. 1) and early AMD–LSI Logic career through Stanford (Ch. 2) are prologue for the 1993 Denny’s founding and the GPU–CUDA–AI arc that sits inside the period. No sister-period copy required for 1946–89 unless a future mining pass wants immigrant-assimilation or 1980s semiconductor-labor context alone.
Overview
The Thinking Machine is Witt’s reported biography of Jensen Huang and Nvidia: how a niche maker of PC graphics accelerators became the hardware backbone of the modern AI boom. The book opens on a 2023 Denny’s breakfast interview (Huang tip $1,000; seven plates), then tracks Huang from Taiwan/Thailand immigration and Appalachian boarding-school trauma through AMD and LSI Logic, the 1993 cofounding with Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem, the near-death NV1 pivot, parallel GPUs for Quake, CUDA as a decade-long Wall Street–defying bet, Toronto’s AlexNet on consumer GeForce cards, the post-2012 all-in on deep learning, transformers and ChatGPT-era hyperscale, and Huang’s near-monopoly on AI training chips as Nvidia’s market value crossed into the trillions. Witt draws on nearly two hundred interviews; Huang cooperates with access but refuses to read the prior New Yorker profile and hopes to “die before” the biography appears.
For this United States 1990–present wiki the source is central to post–Cold War Silicon Valley hardware, the PC gaming industry, fabless semiconductor design with TSMC, private AI infrastructure and cloud hyperscalers, OpenAI/ChatGPT as industrial demand shock, and the public mythology of founder-led chip companies. EPUB structure: Dedication; Epigraph (Marcus Aurelius); Introduction; Part I (Chs. 1–11); Part II (Chs. 12–23); Acknowledgments; About the Author; endnotes; copyright. Brief portions earlier appeared in The New Yorker (2023).
Narrative Source Flow
Introduction
Lines 127–310. Thesis: niche video-game hardware vendor becomes most valuable company; Huang’s thirty-two-year S&P 500 CEO tenure; parallel-computing bet against a “zero percent” historical success rate; 2012 Toronto neural-net breakthrough on consumer cards; Nvidia’s shift from ~200 gaming accessories to multimillion-dollar AI supercomputers powering Midjourney, ChatGPT, Copilot. Denny’s breakfast set piece (Huang as former dishwasher/busboy; “You’re always an immigrant”); Brannan/Gold Rush shovel analogy for 30,000 AI chips; Huang dismisses doomer AI fears (“horses can’t type”; fiction writers first); reporting method (~200 interviews; Huang elusive, self-contradictory, motivated by fear of letting employees down). Closes by pointing back to the 1973 Kentucky arrival.
Part I / Ch. 1 — The Bridge
Lines 313–679. Ten-year-old Jensen arrives Oneida, Kentucky, 1973 with brother Jeff while parents remain in Thailand; rickety footbridge bullying at Oneida Elementary; racial slurs; friendship with Ben Bays; Bruce Lee bluff and determination. Family: Taipei birth February 1963; Bangkok refinery years; mother’s dictionary-word English drills; parents’ plan for U.S. education. Oneida Baptist Institute / cleaning toilets / table tennis; reunification in Oregon; Beaverton high school; Oregon State electrical engineering; lab-partner romance with Lori Mills via homework “superpower”; breadboards to semiconductors; graduation into Silicon Valley chip boom.
Ch. 2 — Large-Scale Integration
Lines 680–1137. Christmas 1984 AMD Moscone party proposal to Lori; overnight drive; black-ice Supra crash near California–Oregon border; neck brace. AMD youth hire ($28,700 starting salary); move to LSI Logic under Wilf Corrigan culture; chip design craft and “large-scale integration”; Stanford master’s while working; friendship with Jens Horstmann; ambition to “run something by the age of thirty”; meeting future cofounders Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem (Sun Microsystems GX graphics; Priem’s intensity); Sega/3D opportunity forming as SGI and Sun ignore consumer PC gaming.
Ch. 3 — New Venture
Lines 1138–1547. 1993 Denny’s San Jose back booth with Malachowsky and Priem; $50M revenue threshold spreadsheet; Jim Gaither incorporation; name “Nvidia” (invidia / envy); Sequoia and early VC; NV1 architecture with Priem’s quadratic mapping vs industry triangles; Sega deal and Diamond Edge boards; Virtua Fighter bundle spike then return-wave failure (no depth buffer; Windows crashes); Christmas-party hubris before 1996 insolvency; Huang documents fab day on VHS; crowded field (3dfx, ATI, S3, Matrox).
Ch. 4 — Thirty Days
Lines 1548–1826. David Kirk’s 1996 arrival: skeleton staff of ~35 after mass layoff; weekly paper checks; hardware emulator in the break room replacing ping-pong table; skip-prototyping gamble to mass-produce a Microsoft-compatible knockoff; Priem vs Huang shouting matches over quadratic mapping as proxy for control; Kirk curbs Priem’s ambitions; NV3 / Riva 128 ships as 128-bit copycat with Swiss-Army features; first smooth 30 fps illusion; company clawback from brink.
Ch. 5 — Going Parallel
Lines 1827–2286. Final day-long Huang–Priem blowup (1998); Apple-mediator comparison (“significantly worse”); Priem demoted to patents, keeps shares; Kirk as consigliere and competitor-brain poacher (Riva demo kills rival firm). Parallel shaders for Carmack’s Quake: twin pipelines on one chip vs 3dfx’s multi-chip cards; Huang converts after first-principles study of Cray/nCube failures; TSMC relationship (Morris Chang; early chemical-process mishap then strategic marriage); Taiwan night-market nostalgia; TNT branding via Dan Vivoli; Carmack endorsement makes Nvidia fetish hardware.
Ch. 6 — Jellyfish
Lines 2287–2568. 1997 Dallas backgammon: Nack Ballard vs Malcolm Davis’s neural-net program Jellyfish—framed as truer dawn of machine age than Kasparov–Deep Blue. History of neural nets from 1940s “nervous nets” through Minsky’s 1969 winter; symbolic AI and expert-systems busts; Gerald Tesauro’s TD-Gammon; Fredrik Dahl’s poker/slots neural work and no-limit hold’em wall. Sets intellectual backdrop for later GPU–neural symbiosis while mainstream AI still scorns the approach.
Ch. 7 — Deathmatch
Lines 2569–3089. Pro gamer Johnathan “fatal1ty” Wendel: 140 ms twitch shots; TNT2 frame-rate edge as Nike-to-Jordan sponsorship analogy. Nvidia’s six-month ship cadence; GeForce (NV10) vs 3dfx Voodoo; patent war, countersuits, and 3dfx’s collapse into asset sale; internal 3dfx view of Huang as Darth Vader; Kirk’s hire list of 120 engineers; “mutate, grow, expand” culture clash with 3dfx play-hard alumni. ATI/Radeon emerges as lasting duopoly rival; programmable shaders and Xbox 2001 deal set up next crisis.
Ch. 8 — The Compulsion Loop
Lines 3090–3410. 2002 table-tennis thwock montage: dot-com crash, leaf-blower GeForce fan, Xbox arbitration collapse, SEC accounting probe; reunion with Joe Romanosky; teppan-grill home life vs Darth Vader office persona. Stock down >90%; Christine Hoberg CFO exit; restatement shows more profit (Coxe: “fishing expedition”). Xbox edge-detection IP fight; Microsoft walks next-gen GPU. Gaming “compulsion loop” / addiction foreshadow; APA “internet gaming disorder” (2013) as coda on the market Nvidia helped build.
Ch. 9 — CUDA
Lines 3411–4010. Ian Buck’s 32× GeForce Quake wall at Stanford → Brook language (DARPA) smuggling science into triangle hardware; Huang hires Buck (2004). SGI decline; Bill Dally courtship begins. John Nickolls invents CUDA—“video game card on every scientist’s desk”; free 2006 launch; “CUDA tax” vs Radeon; gamers subsidize R&D; mammogram alpha tests; Wall Street hostility; Nickolls’s dying insistence CUDA will change the world. Debi Shoquist packaging expedite (“That’s the right answer”); CUDA as platform lock-in seeking a killer app.
Ch. 10 — Resonance
Lines 4011–4434. Bill Dally portrait: patents, plane ditching in Long Island Sound, MIT Jellybean parallel machine, Stanford chair; turns down Intel to join money-losing Nvidia (2009) as chief scientist—“Intel is going to crush Nvidia.” Moore’s Law leakage; Jeff Smith / Starboard Value raid (Olive Garden playbook); Huang doubles down on CUDA despite “money pit” perception; Icera mobile misstep as raid trigger. Thesis: ship CUDA on every retail card to find the “lunatic” whose neglected science needs the firepower—resonance between architecture and unknown workload.
Ch. 11 — AlexNet
Lines 4435–4845. Geoffrey Hinton’s Toronto outcasts; Alex Krizhevsky (best programmer Hinton met) and Ilya Sutskever; neural nets as ideological pariah; “machine learning” rebrand. Two GeForce GTX 580s in a bedroom; ImageNet; SuperVision / AlexNet crushes 2012 contest (~85% vs ~70% prior SOTA); Fei-Fei Li’s disbelief (Honda Civic land-speed analogy); Google replication (WojNet) and talent war; Hinton: without CUDA, too much trouble. Closes Part I: two failed underdog technologies finally pay off together.
Part II / Ch. 12 — O.I.A.L.O.
Lines 4848–5223. Bryan Catanzaro (Russian lit + circuits; Siberia mission; Intel Larrabee intern who saw Moore’s wall) becomes AI-from-below prophet; parking-lot draft for cuDNN team. Huang’s Friday email: no longer a graphics company—by Monday an AI company. Whiteboard acronym O.I.A.L.O. = “Once in a Lifetime Opportunity.” Matrix-multiply / fuzzy weights / inference vs training; Philippe Vandermersch as “Wozniak” to Catanzaro’s Jobs; GTC 2014 first public AI association; Starboard doubles money and vanishes.
Ch. 13 — Superintelligence
Lines 5224–5653. Post-fifty Huang abandons hobbies, movies, teppan; only AI. Stock finally clears 2001 S&P peak; cloud hyperscalers (Google Mack Truck GPU buys; Amazon, Microsoft, Oracle) build rack-scale GPU utilities. DGX / Pascal P100: compute faster than data can arrive; “computer” transcends arithmetic bottleneck. Internal culture of speed-of-light schedules and zero-billion-dollar markets; Huang’s fifty-plus direct reports and no successor.
Ch. 14 — The Good Year
Lines 5654–6150. 2016–17 glory: Nvidia +224% then AMD +309% under cousin Lisa Su (first cousin once removed; tiger-parent New York path); private trash-talk vs public courtesy; 2006 AMD merger talks die when Huang won’t give up CEO chair. Product blizzard; Isaac → Omniverse simulation stack; reality-simulator as classic Huang zero-billion-dollar bet; GeForce/Radeon share wars.
Ch. 15 — The Transformer
Lines 6151–6546. Jakob Uszkoreit at Google: self-attention, tokens, design-for-GPU vs recurrent nets; “Attention Is All You Need” lineage; Sutskever watches two leaps (AlexNet, transformer) and hunts the next. Large language models; Huang orders Bas Aarts to scrap RNN compiler tooling for transformer stack; OpenAI / Microsoft scale as demand signal.
Ch. 16 — Hyperscale
Lines 6547–6810. Huang’s scale gospel: AI as software on sold hardware, not mystical superintelligence; GTC “supercharged law” (AlexNet week → DGX-2 eighteen minutes). Mellanox / Infiniband acquisition (~$7B, 2019–20) after Starboard raids Waldman—data-center nervous system; “Nvidia Israel”; Stevens: one of recent memory’s most profitable deals. Networking as synergy that turns GPU piles into one chip.
Ch. 17 — Money
Lines 6811–7087. GPT-3 training-data controversies (Wikipedia, Times archives, suspected Books2/LibGen); ChatGPT Nov 2022 viral launch; GPT-4 exam scores and napkin-to-website demos; Witt’s job anxiety. Equity windfalls for early Nvidia hands (Kirk’s “more money than I ever thought”); opaque Priem fortune; Microsoft’s $10B+ OpenAI stake; AI as spiritual first-use experience (Sutskever).
Ch. 18 — Spaceships
Lines 7088–7326. Voyager campus tour: black “mountain,” vertical gardens, AI janitor dispatch cameras; employees beatified as market cap hits ~$3T; QC labs as dwarves in the mountain. Ray tracing / photoreal ramen shop; “Diane” avatar blackheads; Huang’s goal to unify graphics and generative AI into inhabitable worlds. Catanzaro’s anti–sci-fi close: AI won’t play zero-sum with humans.
Ch. 19 — Power
Lines 7327–7517. Dominion Energy live-line work in Loudoun County, Virginia—data-center capital; inference (not only training) drives load; Google search energy 10× with generative AI; nuclear and coal revival talk vs climate-modeling irony. James Earl Jones voice clone; radiologist/farm-robot labor displacement; Elliott Management 2024 bubble warning on tech/Nvidia; vaporware enterprise AI.
Ch. 20 — The Most Important Stock on Earth
Lines 7518–7955. Feb 21–22, 2024 earnings Judgment Day: ~60B revenue, >70% gross margin, ~30B net (~prior thirty years combined); $277B single-day market-cap gain; Goldman’s “most important stock on earth.” Huang as Edison of AI factories; fifty-five direct reports, no successor; Glassdoor #1 employer; “life’s work” career framing; two fringe fields (parallel computing + neural nets) fused toward sentience.
Ch. 21 — Jensen
Lines 7956–8220. Cult of mononym “Jensen”; leather-jacket visionary slot after Jobs; struggle sessions and catchphrase catechism (“speed of light,” “zero-billion-dollar market”); self-contradiction as real-time thinking; Hao Ko wardrobe roast; $100B+ “Do you know how rich I am?” not as boast but unsettled inventory. Leadership: chaotic, dictatorial, never boring.
Ch. 22 — The Fear
Lines 8221–8603. Yoshua Bengio’s 2023 Montreal “conversion” walk after ChatGPT; extinction fear worse than nuclear (designer pathogen); Hinton quits Google; Sutskever on alignment—top-cited trio alarmed. Yann LeCun as skeptic foil. Contrast with Huang’s unshaken optimism; industry open letters Huang won’t sign; doomerism among the Toronto lineage that first proved GPUs for deep learning.
Ch. 23 — The Thinking Machine
Lines 8604–8833. Post–GTC 2024 final interview: whiteboard office wrapped in stack diagrams; Oppenheimer / FTC / French raid pressure. Arthur C. Clarke clip detonates Huang—rage against sci-fi framing, job-destruction questions, therapy-style biography; “serious people doing serious work.” Eos 10,000-chip supercomputer tour (GPT-3 trained in <4 minutes); Witt’s coda: executives fear Jensen’s yell more than human extinction; American Daedalus seeing atom-to-consciousness stack; the thinking machine getting smarter with each fan spin.
